cells.tense: You are standing where something has just finished, and the next thing is already arriving.
cells.ask: Tell one person one thing that has actually finished for you, and leave it finished. No next chapter, no lesson added on.
cells.core: You can close a thing and stay open at the same time. That's the rare part. Most people either grip the ending or sprint past it, but you can let a chapter complete and still meet what's arriving without forcing it to hurry. Nothing held shut, nothing rushed through. You recognize the turning while you're inside it, and that recognition is quiet and unglamorous.\n\nSo today, when something is done, let it be done. What's coming in next doesn't need your help crossing over. It's timing, not effort. You can watch what's arriving and meet it at the speed it's arriving. The practice is small and repeatable at any hour: stay here while both sides move, and let the new thing take its own shape without your hand on it.
cells.sheetLine: You can close a thing and still stay open to what's next.
cells.verb: letting what has gathered finish, and meeting what comes in behind it
cells.place: the threshold where what was outside is coming in

cells.tense: You are already bracing past the end of something that hasn't ended yet.
cells.ask: Pick one unfinished thing and stop calling it done this week — even just to yourself. Leave it open and live next to it a few more days.
cells.core: At its plain best this is unglamorous: you notice what's actually arriving and meet it where it stands. No pushing, no pre-writing the next step first. The thing takes the shape it takes, and you're there for it, keeping pace with it instead of the pace in your head.\n\nThat isn't what's happening now. You've laid the last tile and the floor isn't finished. In your head the project is behind you and the next one has started, but the actual thing is still mid-sentence. What it costs you is the last stretch, which is where a thing is really completed. Slow to what's here and let the ending do its ending.
cells.sheetLine: You've declared the ending before the ending has happened.
cells.verb: letting what has gathered finish, and meeting what comes in behind it
cells.place: the threshold where what was outside is coming in

cells.tense: You were standing at a door that already opened, and you are still there.
cells.ask: Name one thing that finished a while back — small, real — and do one thing that treats it as over. One act, not a whole ritual.
cells.core: When this one is running right, you let a thing complete without needing to see the next one first. You can stand at the moment something ends and not reach past it. The arrival comes when it comes, and you're here for it. Closing doesn't take anything away from you, and you don't have to brace for that.\n\nThat isn't what's happening now. Things keep almost finishing. You get close, then look for the next one before the first one lands, and there's a pile of nearly-done sitting next to you. Closing feels like losing something, so you keep it open. Let one thing be done and your hands come back. Not fate. Just timing.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it open because closing feels like losing it.
cells.verb: letting what has gathered finish, and meeting what comes in behind it
cells.place: the threshold where what was outside is coming in

cells.tense: You are already writing the next page and calling it someone else's hand.
cells.ask: Say plainly, once, that you ended something — out loud to one person, or written where you'll see it. Just state it. Don't explain it.
cells.core: Running well, this knows when a thing has run its course and lets it go without ceremony. You can stand at the end of something and name it finished, then turn toward what's coming in. That's not defeat — that's how the next thing gets a clean opening. Letting go and finishing are the same motion, and you don't have to make a lesson out of it.\n\nThat isn't what's happening now. Some things around you ended — a job, a pattern, a way you used to be — and you describe them as things that happened to you. You don't claim the ending. But you're the one who stopped showing up, who changed the pattern, who let it go. Name it once and the doorway clears.
cells.sheetLine: You ended it. You keep describing it as something that happened to you.
